plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 23: Gauss's Law
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional sketch of a small cylindrical Gaussian surface straddling the surface of a charged conductor. The conductor's surface is drawn as a broad, softly shaded lavender sheet receding into the distance, sprinkled with plus signs and labeled 'sigma' at the upper left. A short translucent cyan cylinder stands through the sheet with its axis along the surface normal, one flat end face above the surface and the other below it, and its curved side wall shown in cross-section. The center of the cylinder is marked by a small black dot labeled P lying on the surface itself. A red arrow labeled with a vector E rises from the upper end face along the cylinder axis, and a curved leader from the right names that face 'Delta A'. A second curved leader from the lower left points at the buried portion and labels it 'E = 0'. A bracketed dimension at the left, labeled 'delta', gives the cylinder's height. Setting the outward arrow against the vanishing field below is the point of the drawing: flux crosses only the outer end cap. The construction supports relating the field just outside a conductor in equilibrium to the local surface charge density.

elements: broad conductor surface plane (horizontal XZ plane at Y=0) with soft lavender-to-white radial shading
scattered '+' charge symbols distributed across the conductor surface
surface charge density label 'σ' at the upper-left of the plane
translucent cyan Gaussian pillbox cylinder, axis along the surface normal (+Y), straddling the plane
top (outer) flat end cap of the cylinder above the surface
bottom (inner/buried) flat end cap of the cylinder below the surface
curved side wall of the cylinder
small black dot at the cylinder center on the surface, labeled 'P'
red vector arrow labeled 'E' rising from the top cap along +Y (the surface normal)
curved leader line from the right naming the top cap 'ΔA'
curved leader line from the lower-left naming the buried portion 'E = 0'
vertical dimension bracket on the left of the cylinder labeled 'δ' giving its height

interactions.label: Pillbox height δ
interactions.teaches: Thinning the cylinder shrinks the side-wall area toward zero while the outer cap keeps the only nonzero E arrow, showing that in the δ→0 limit the side wall contributes no flux and only the outer cap carries E·ΔA

interactions.label: Field region
interactions.teaches: Switching regions makes the conductor boundary condition visible: just outside the surface E is perpendicular to it, while everywhere inside the conductor in equilibrium E = 0, so the buried cap and the interior portion of the wall carry zero flux

Clicking the top cap, side wall, or buried cap highlights that surface and reveals its flux term (E·ΔA, 0, 0), clarifying that the total flux reduces to the single outer-cap term that Gauss's law equates to σΔA/ε0, hence E = σ/ε0

demo_steps.title: Pillbox straddling the surface
demo_steps.narration: A short Gaussian cylinder of height δ stands through the charged conductor with point P on the surface. The red E arrow leaves only the outer cap; the buried half sits where E = 0.

demo_steps.title: Thin the pillbox
demo_steps.narration: Drag δ down toward 0.2. The side wall's area collapses, so its flux vanishes; the only surviving flux is E·ΔA through the outer cap.

demo_steps.title: Inspect each surface's flux
demo_steps.narration: Click the top cap, side wall, and buried cap in turn. Their flux terms read E·ΔA, 0, and 0 — the boundary condition E = σ/ε0 follows from the single nonzero term.

demo_steps.title: Inside the conductor
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the inside region: the field arrow disappears below the surface and the buried cap is labeled E = 0, confirming no flux crosses the inner half of the pillbox.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World space: conductor surface is the horizontal XZ plane at Y=0, spanning X ∈ [-4, 4] and Z ∈ [-4, 4], rendered as a large plane with a radial lavender gradient (center ~#c9c9ec fading to near-white #f4f4fb at the rim). '+' symbols are small black crosses scattered at Y=0 over roughly X,Z ∈ [-3.5, 3.5], ~20 of them. The pillbox is a cylinder of radius 0.6 world units centered at the origin with axis along +Y; its height equals δ (default 1.2), so top cap at Y=+δ/2 and bottom cap at Y=-δ/2. Cylinder material translucent cyan #7fd6d6 at ~0.4 opacity with a slightly brighter top cap. Point P is a black sphere ~0.05 at the origin on the surface. The E vector is a red #cc2222 arrow from the top-cap center (0, δ/2, 0) pointing +Y, length ~1.0, with label 'E' at its tip. The δ bracket is a thin black double-arrow line at X ≈ -0.9 spanning Y ∈ [-δ/2, +δ/2]. Leaders for 'ΔA' (right) and 'E = 0' (lower-left) are thin curved black lines. Dominant palette: lavender sheet, teal cylinder, red arrow, black labels/symbols. Physics: total flux Φ = E·ΔA = σΔA/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/ε0.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the cylinder from three pickable meshes (top cap disc, bottom cap disc, open side wall via CylinderGeometry with openEnded or separate tube) so click-selection can highlight one part by swapping its material emissive/opacity. Recompute cap Y-positions and the δ bracket reactively on slider change; keep radius fixed. On the fieldRegion toggle, show/hide the red E arrow and swap the buried-cap annotation between 'E = 0' emphasis and neutral. Use a low-to-moderate elevation axonometric pose so the plane reads as a receding sheet and the cylinder stands upright through it, matching the source's grazing diagonal sweep. Render '+' symbols as instanced small cross geometries lying flat on the plane.

authoredContext:
To see this, consider an infinitesimally small Gaussian cylinder that surrounds a point on the surface of the conductor, as in the figure. The cylinder has one end face inside and one end face outside the surface. The height and cross-sectional area of the cylinder are δ and ΔA, respectively. The cylinder’s sides are perpendicular to the surface of the conductor, and its end faces are parallel to the surface. Because the cylinder is infinitesimally small, the charge density σ is essentially constant over the surface enclosed, so the total charge inside the Gaussian cylinder is σΔA. Now E is perpendicular to the surface of the conductor outside the conductor and vanishes within it, because otherwise, the charges would accelerate, and we would not be in equilibrium. Electric flux therefore crosses only the outer end face of the Gaussian surface and may be written as EΔA, since the cylinder is assumed to be small enough that E is approximately constant over that area. From Gauss’ law,

Thus,

An infinitesimally small cylindrical Gaussian surface surrounds point P, which is on the surface of the conductor. The field E→ is perpendicular to the surface of the conductor outside the conductor and vanishes within it.

A surface labeled sigma has plus signs on it. A point P on the surface forms the center of a cylinder. An arrow labeled vector E is along the axis of the cylinder and emerges from its top surface. The top surface of the cylinder is labeled delta A and the bottom surface is labeled vector E equal to zero. These are parallel to the surface sigma. The length of the cylinder is labeled sigma.

For a conductor with a cavity, if we put a charge +q inside the cavity, then the charge separation takes place in the conductor, with −q amount of charge on the inside surface and a +q amount of charge at the outside surface (the figure(a)). For the same conductor with a charge +q outside it, there is no excess charge on the inside surface; both the positive and negative induced charges reside on the outside surface (the figure(b)).

The center of the cylinder is marked by a small black dot labeled P lying on the surface itself. A red arrow labeled with a vector E rises from the upper end face along the cylinder axis, and a curved leader from the right names that face 'Delta A'. interactions.label: Pillbox height δ
interactions.teaches: Thinning the cylinder shrinks the side-wall area toward zero while the outer cap keeps the only nonzero E arrow, showing that in the δ→0 limit the side wall contributes no flux and only the outer cap carries E·ΔA

interactions.label: Field region
interactions.teaches: Switching regions makes the conductor boundary condition visible: just outside the surface E is perpendicular to it, while everywhere inside the conductor in equilibrium E = 0, so the buried cap and the interior portion of the wall carry zero flux

Clicking the top cap, side wall, or buried cap highlights that surface and reveals its flux term (E·ΔA, 0, 0), clarifying that the total flux reduces to the single outer-cap term that Gauss's law equates to σΔA/ε0, hence E = σ/ε0

demo_steps.title: Pillbox straddling the surface
demo_steps.narration: A short Gaussian cylinder of height δ stands through the charged conductor with point P on the surface. The red E arrow leaves only the outer cap; the buried half sits where E = 0.

demo_steps.title: Thin the pillbox
demo_steps.narration: Drag δ down toward 0.2. The side wall's area collapses, so its flux vanishes; the only surviving flux is E·ΔA through the outer cap.

demo_steps.title: Inspect each surface's flux
demo_steps.narration: Click the top cap, side wall, and buried cap in turn. Their flux terms read E·ΔA, 0, and 0 — the boundary condition E = σ/ε0 follows from the single nonzero term.

demo_steps.title: Inside the conductor
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the inside region: the field arrow disappears below the surface and the buried cap is labeled E = 0, confirming no flux crosses the inner half of the pillbox.
